analogy.p: Imagine metal ions and hydroxide ions as dancers wandering freely around a ballroom. When the right partners meet, they lock into a fixed pattern and leave the dance floor as a solid: the precipitate. Copper(II) needs two hydroxide partners, aluminium and iron(III) need three, and the colour of the couple tells you who they are. Aluminium is the odd one out: when many extra partners arrive it breaks the pattern and rejoins the crowd (it redissolves). The analogy breaks down because ions are held by electrostatic attraction rather than choice, and in a solid they are packed in a giant lattice rather than in separate pairs.
analogy.t: Dancers pairing up in a ballroom

bullets: Reagent: **sodium hydroxide solution, NaOH(aq)**, added first dropwise and then in excess.
Observation to record: the **colour of the precipitate** and whether it **dissolves in excess**.
Ions in the specification: Al³⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.
This is **triple (separate science) content only**: combined-science students do not need it.
The test finds the **metal cation**; it does not identify the negative ion (anion) in the compound.
Typically examined on **Paper 2** as a 2 to 6 mark question on identifying an unknown or writing an equation.
Link: flame tests and instrumental methods (flame emission spectroscopy) are other ways to identify metal ions.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know (triple science)
core.p: AQA Chemistry (triple only) expects you to describe how sodium hydroxide solution is used to identify some metal ions. When NaOH(aq) is added to a solution containing certain metal ions, an insoluble metal hydroxide forms as a **precipitate**. You must know the colour of the precipitate for **aluminium, calcium and magnesium** (all white), **copper(II)** (blue), **iron(II)** (green) and **iron(III)** (brown). You must also know that the **aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide** to give a colourless solution, whereas calcium and magnesium hydroxide do not. Finally you should be able to write balanced and ionic equations for the reactions.

bullets: A **precipitate** is an **insoluble solid formed when two solutions react**.
General word equation: metal salt + sodium hydroxide → metal hydroxide (precipitate) + sodium salt.
The reaction happens because the **metal hydroxide is insoluble**; if no insoluble product could form there would be no visible change.
Spectator ions are present on both sides of the equation and are left out of the **ionic equation**.
The precipitate is made of the **metal ion and hydroxide ions in a fixed ratio** set by their charges, e.g. Cu²⁺ needs 2OH⁻.
The solid is **suspended** at first, then may settle at the bottom of the tube on standing.
Link to other topics: solubility of salts, making insoluble salts by precipitation, and ionic bonding.
core.p: Most ionic compounds containing Na⁺ are soluble, so adding NaOH(aq) supplies a high concentration of **hydroxide ions, OH⁻**. Many metal hydroxides are **insoluble** in water. When metal ions meet hydroxide ions they attract strongly and pack together into a giant ionic lattice, which is a solid that is too heavy to stay dissolved. This tiny suspended solid makes the mixture cloudy: it is called a **precipitate**, and the reaction is a **precipitation reaction**. The sodium ions and the original negative ions (such as chloride or sulfate) do not take part, so they are **spectator ions**.

bullets: Place about **2 cm depth** of the solution to be tested into a test tube.
Add **sodium hydroxide solution dropwise** and note the colour of any precipitate that forms.
Continue adding NaOH until it is **in excess**, shaking gently, and note whether the precipitate **dissolves**.
If the precipitate is white and dissolves, the ion is **Al³⁺**; if white and it does not dissolve, the ion is **Mg²⁺ or Ca²⁺**.
Use a **clean dropper** for each sample, or contamination gives false results.
Hazard: sodium hydroxide is **corrosive**; control risk with **eye protection** and dilute solutions.
Record results in a table: ion, colour of precipitate, effect of excess NaOH.
Use a white background behind the tube so pale precipitates are easier to see.
core.p: The test is quick and needs only a few cm³ of the sample. The key skill is adding the NaOH **a few drops at a time** so that you see the first precipitate form, and then adding more until the NaOH is in **excess**, so you can see whether the precipitate dissolves. Always observe and record before adding more. Use dilute sodium hydroxide, wear eye protection (it is corrosive and irritant to the eyes and skin) and wash spills with plenty of water.

bullets: **Aluminium, Al³⁺** → **white** precipitate of aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)₃; **dissolves in excess** NaOH.
**Calcium, Ca²⁺** → **white** precipitate of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂; **does not dissolve** in excess.
**Magnesium, Mg²⁺** → **white** precipitate of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂; **does not dissolve** in excess.
**Copper(II), Cu²⁺** → **blue** precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide, Cu(OH)₂.
**Iron(II), Fe²⁺** → **green** precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₂.
**Iron(III), Fe³⁺** → **brown** precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₃.
Memory aid: Cu is **blue**, Fe(II) is **green**, Fe(III) is **brown** (rust-coloured, like rust itself).
Only **aluminium** gives a precipitate that redissolves; this is the one fact that separates it from Mg and Ca.
core.p: Learn the table below. Three ions give a white precipitate, so a white result is not enough to identify one ion on its own; you need the excess test and, if required, a flame test. The coloured precipitates come from **transition metal ions**, which form coloured compounds. Notice that iron has two possible ions: iron(II) gives a **green** precipitate and iron(III) gives a **brown** precipitate, so the test can tell you which oxidation state of iron is present.

bullets: Step 1: add NaOH dropwise → **white precipitate** (Al³⁺, Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺).
Step 2: add **excess** NaOH → if the precipitate **dissolves**, the ion is **Al³⁺**.
Step 3: if it does **not** dissolve, the ion is **Mg²⁺ or Ca²⁺**.
Step 4: **flame test** on the original sample: **Ca²⁺ is orange-red**, Mg²⁺ gives no flame colour.
The final solution with aluminium is **colourless**, not clear and white: say 'colourless'.
In the flame test, a **nichrome or platinum wire** is cleaned in acid first to avoid contamination.
Sodium ions in the NaOH reagent mean you can **never** test for Na⁺ with this method; use a flame test instead.
Mark scheme phrase: 'white precipitate that **redissolves / dissolves in excess** sodium hydroxide to form a colourless solution'.
core.p: Aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions all give white precipitates, so you need a second step. Adding **excess** sodium hydroxide dissolves aluminium hydroxide, giving a **colourless solution**, while calcium and magnesium hydroxides remain as solids. To separate calcium from magnesium you cannot use sodium hydroxide alone, but a **flame test** works: calcium gives an **orange-red** flame, whereas magnesium compounds give no distinctive flame colour. This is a good example of combining two tests to identify an ion, which is exactly the reasoning examiners reward.

bullets: Aluminium hydroxide is **amphoteric**: it reacts with both acids and strong alkalis (beyond the GCSE requirement, but helps you remember).
In excess NaOH, the precipitate **redissolves** because a soluble aluminium-containing ion forms.
The final mixture is a **colourless solution**, so the white solid has gone.
Mg(OH)₂ and Ca(OH)₂ are **basic hydroxides**, so there is no further reaction with NaOH.
If an exam asks 'what is seen', write **'white precipitate forms, then dissolves in excess giving a colourless solution'**.
A common error is to say the precipitate 'disappears' without saying the solution is colourless.
Link to other topics: acids and bases, and how reactivity patterns link to hydroxide behaviour.
core.p: Aluminium hydroxide is different because it can react with both acids and alkalis, a property called being **amphoteric**. With a little NaOH it forms the insoluble hydroxide, but with extra hydroxide ions the aluminium hydroxide reacts further to form a soluble complex ion, so the white solid disappears. You do not need the formula of this soluble species for GCSE, only the observation. Calcium and magnesium hydroxides are basic only, so they do not react with extra NaOH and remain as solids.

bullets: **Cu²⁺** gives a **blue** gelatinous precipitate; the solid is **copper(II) hydroxide**.
**Fe²⁺** gives a **green** precipitate; the solid is **iron(II) hydroxide**.
**Fe³⁺** gives a **brown** precipitate; the solid is **iron(III) hydroxide**.
The number in brackets, e.g. **iron(II)**, is the **charge on the ion** (2+ or 3+).
Transition metal compounds are often **coloured**, unlike most group 1 and 2 compounds.
The precipitate formula depends on the **charge**: Fe²⁺ needs 2OH⁻, Fe³⁺ needs 3OH⁻.
Green iron(II) hydroxide can turn **brown at the surface in air** as it is oxidised to iron(III).
Do not confuse **green Fe²⁺** with **brown Fe³⁺**: they are the commonest lost mark.
core.p: Copper, iron(II) and iron(III) are transition metals, and their hydroxides are coloured. The blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide forms from a blue solution, so the colour change is subtle: the tube changes from a clear blue solution to a cloudy blue mixture with a solid. Iron(II) hydroxide is green and iron(III) hydroxide is brown. Iron(II) compounds can be slowly oxidised by air to iron(III), so a green precipitate may develop brown patches on standing. None of these precipitates dissolves in excess NaOH at GCSE level.

bullets: Al³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Al(OH)₃(s)
Mg²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Mg(OH)₂(s)  and  Ca²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Ca(OH)₂(s)
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s)
Fe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s)  and  Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s)
Full example: CuSO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) + Na₂SO₄(aq).
Full example: FeCl₃(aq) + 3NaOH(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s) + 3NaCl(aq).
Check balance of **atoms and charge**: the charges on each side of an ionic equation must add up to the same total.
Always include **state symbols**: (aq) for ions in solution and (s) for the precipitate.
core.p: To write an equation, balance the charges. A hydroxide ion has a charge of 1−, so the number of OH⁻ ions in the formula equals the charge on the metal ion. This gives Al(OH)₃, Ca(OH)₂, Mg(OH)₂, Cu(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₂ and Fe(OH)₃. For the full equation, the metal salt and NaOH are aqueous, the hydroxide is solid, and sodium salt stays aqueous. For the ionic equation, cross out spectator ions: the ionic equation is always metal ion + hydroxide ions → metal hydroxide (s). Higher tier questions often ask for the ionic equation with state symbols.

bullets: Say **'a (colour) precipitate forms'**; do not write 'it goes cloudy' only.
Use **colourless** (not 'clear') for a solution with no colour.
For 'identify the ion', give the **name and formula with charge**, e.g. 'aluminium ions, Al³⁺'.
Link evidence to conclusion in one sentence: **observation → ion**.
Describe the **order of tests** for a question worth 4 or 6 marks.
Mention **dropwise** and **excess** in method answers.
Do not say 'the NaOH identifies the ion', say 'the **colour of the precipitate** identifies the ion'.
core.h: Observation language and what examiners want
core.p: Examiners want precise observation words. A **precipitate** is a solid forming in a solution, so say 'a blue precipitate forms', not 'it goes blue' or 'it turns into a solid'. Colours must be exact: 'white', 'blue', 'green', 'brown'. If the question asks you to explain how you know, link observation to conclusion: 'the white precipitate dissolved in excess, so the ion is aluminium'. Avoid using the word 'clear' to mean colourless in a way that confuses: 'colourless solution' is the safest wording.

bullets: The test is **qualitative only**: it does not give concentration.
Three ions give a **white** precipitate, so extra tests are needed.
**Group 1 ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Li⁺)** do not form precipitates because their hydroxides are soluble.
A **mixture** of ions can mask colours or give mixed precipitates.
The test needs a **fairly high concentration** of the ion to see a precipitate.
Instrumental methods are **rapid, sensitive and accurate**, and need only small samples.
Disadvantage of instrumental methods: **expensive equipment** and trained operators.
core.p: The sodium hydroxide test has limitations. White precipitates cannot be told apart by this test alone, mixtures of metal ions give confusing results, and the test is **qualitative** because it does not tell you how much of the ion is present. It also cannot detect ions such as sodium and potassium, because their hydroxides are soluble. Instrumental methods such as flame emission spectroscopy are faster, more sensitive and can identify several ions at once, which is why industry uses them for large numbers of samples.

bullets: **Water treatment**: heavy metal ions removed as hydroxide precipitates.
**Insoluble salts** can be made by precipitation, then filtered, washed and dried.
Links to **ionic bonding** and **formulae from ion charges**.
Links to **ionic equations** and the idea of spectator ions.
Links to **identifying ions** more widely: flame tests, anion tests and instrumental methods.
Links to the **reactivity series**: group 1 hydroxides are soluble, many others are not.
Links to **transition metals**: coloured compounds and ions with different charges.
core.h: Applications and links to other topics
core.p: Precipitation of metal hydroxides is useful beyond testing. In water treatment, alkali can be added to remove dissolved heavy metal ions as insoluble hydroxides which are then filtered out. In the lab, the same idea is used to make insoluble salts. It connects ionic bonding (why the lattice forms), writing formulae from charges, and ionic equations, all of which are tested at GCSE. Understanding it also supports the transition metal topic and the identification of unknown substances.

bullets: Order your answer as **test → observation → conclusion**.
If more than one ion fits, say **'could be Mg²⁺ or Ca²⁺'** and give the next test.
Use the **equation ratio** to find mass of precipitate: moles of ion = moles of hydroxide formed (1:1 for Cu²⁺).
Check units: mass in **g**, moles in **mol**, volume in **dm³** when using concentration × volume.
Always state **which tests would be needed next** if an ion has not been fully identified.
core.h: Higher tier style reasoning: working out the ion
core.p: Questions often give you results from a series of tests and ask you to decide which ion is present. Work systematically: first the colour, then excess NaOH, then any extra test given. For a 6 mark question, name each test, give the expected observation and state the conclusion; that structure is exactly what the mark scheme uses. Be clear about reasoning: when two ions could fit an observation, say so and explain what further test separates them. If a numerical element appears, use moles: moles = mass ÷ Mr, and use the equation ratio to find the mass of precipitate.

exam: Command word **'Describe'** (2 marks): give the colour of the precipitate and, if relevant, what happens in excess; one mark per observation.
**'Identify the ion'** (1 mark): give the name and formula with its charge, e.g. 'copper(II), Cu²⁺'.
**'Write an ionic equation'** (2 to 3 marks): correct ions, balanced hydroxide ratio, and state symbols.
**'Explain'** questions need a reason: 'because an **insoluble** hydroxide forms'.
For 4 mark questions on a series of tests, write **test, observation, conclusion** for each step.
For a 6 mark 'plan an investigation' answer, include **dropwise addition, excess NaOH, observations, a table of results and a safety precaution**.
Use exact phrases: **'white precipitate'**, **'dissolves in excess to form a colourless solution'**, **'brown precipitate'**.
If asked to **distinguish Mg²⁺ from Ca²⁺**, say sodium hydroxide cannot do it and use a **flame test**.
Always read tables of results carefully: tick off each test against each ion before concluding.
State symbols: **(aq)** for ions, **(s)** for hydroxides; leaving them out can lose a mark.
If the question says 'a student' made an error, look for **'added too much too quickly'** or **'dirty dropper'**.

mistakes.r: Iron(II) hydroxide is **green** and iron(III) hydroxide is **brown**.
mistakes.w: Iron(II) hydroxide is brown and iron(III) is green.

mistakes.r: The white aluminium hydroxide precipitate **dissolves in excess** NaOH to give a colourless solution.
mistakes.w: Aluminium gives a white solid that stays when excess NaOH is added.

mistakes.r: Al³⁺, Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ all give a white precipitate; excess NaOH and a flame test are needed to tell them apart.
mistakes.w: A white precipitate means the ion must be aluminium.

mistakes.r: The precipitate **dissolves** to form a **colourless solution**.
mistakes.w: The solution goes clear / the precipitate disappears.

mistakes.r: The reagent contains sodium and group 1 hydroxides are soluble, so use a **flame test** for Na⁺.
mistakes.w: Sodium hydroxide can be used to test for sodium ions.

mistakes.r: Use the charge to get the formula: Cu(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₃, Al(OH)₃.
mistakes.w: Fe(OH)₂ for iron(III) hydroxide, or Cu(OH) for copper.

mistakes.r: The precipitate is the **metal hydroxide**; the sodium salt (e.g. Na₂SO₄) stays dissolved.
mistakes.w: The precipitate is the sodium salt.

mistakes.r: Remove spectator ions and include (aq) and (s), e.g. Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s).
mistakes.w: Ionic equation without state symbols or with spectator ions.

summary: You need to know that adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution of metal ions forms insoluble metal hydroxide precipitates with characteristic colours: white for aluminium, calcium and magnesium (only aluminium redissolves in excess), blue for copper(II), green for iron(II) and brown for iron(III). It matters because it lets you identify an unknown metal ion and write ionic equations in Paper 2.

worked.ans: FeCl₃(aq) + 3NaOH(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s) + 3NaCl(aq); ionic: Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s). The brown precipitate is iron(III) hydroxide.
worked.q: Write the balanced equation, with state symbols, and the ionic equation for iron(III) chloride solution reacting with sodium hydroxide solution. (3 marks)
steps: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻, so iron(III) chloride is FeCl₃.
Fe³⁺ needs three OH⁻, so the precipitate is Fe(OH)₃.
Balance Na and Cl: FeCl₃(aq) + 3NaOH(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s) + 3NaCl(aq).
Remove spectator ions Na⁺ and Cl⁻ to get the ionic equation.

worked.ans: X contains aluminium ions, Al³⁺. A white precipitate of aluminium hydroxide formed, and it dissolved in excess sodium hydroxide to form a colourless solution; magnesium and calcium hydroxides do not dissolve in excess.
worked.q: A solution X gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide. The precipitate dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide is added. Identify the metal ion in X and explain your reasoning. (3 marks)
steps: White precipitate narrows it to Al³⁺, Mg²⁺ or Ca²⁺.
Only aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess NaOH.
Mg(OH)₂ and Ca(OH)₂ remain as solids.

worked.q: 0.0100 mol of copper(II) sulfate reacts with excess sodium hydroxide. Calculate the mass of copper(II) hydroxide formed. (Ar: Cu = 63.5, O = 16, H = 1) (3 marks)
steps: CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂ + Na₂SO₄ so the ratio CuSO₄ : Cu(OH)₂ is 1 : 1.
